memories.memory_text: I noticed the discoloration on the wall and realized the painting was gone, which made me panic and tell someone to call the police.
I saw Flan find the Kandinsky painting leaning against a chair, and I felt the tension lift when he pointed it out.
I chose to hang the geometric side of the Kandinsky painting, the quieter one, and stood back to admire how it settled the room.
I saw Flan checking the office, making sure things like the slide projector were still there, and I remember him pointing out the silver beaver inkwell, asking why it mattered.
I saw Flan bury his face in his hands before saying we had to go to the wedding, as if it were some sudden burden he remembered.
I remember Flan telling me we had to go to a wedding later that day, but I told him I was in no mood to go.
I told Flan I am in no mood to go to any wedding, and when he insisted, I reminded him they're his friends, not mine, feeling the weight of his expectation pressing on me.
I heard Flan call out 'Hello?' and I ran to him in terror, certain someone was still in the apartment, and he held me tightly.

I ran out of our apartment with Flan, my clothes barely on and my face still numb with shock, rushing down the side street to the garage and jumping into the passenger seat of our Mercedes as we fled to nowhere I could name.
I heard Flan say he was shaking, and it worried me because we were in the car and he was driving.
I offered to drive instead because I could see he wasn't steady, and I felt I had to step in.
He told me he had to hang on, so I knew he didn't want to let go of the wheel, even though I wasn't sure he should keep driving.
I was in the car with Flan during the day, and we were having a tense conversation while he drove too fast and I put on a tape.
I remember when a car suddenly veered close to us, and I saw Flan swerve sharply to avoid it.
I demanded to take over driving because Flan was driving dangerously.
I went in the room first, and I made sure to say it because it mattered.
I saw Flan snap off the tape deck abruptly while we were arguing.
I heard Flan shout that it was Maria Callas's fault when the truck nearly hit us.
I ran up to the bride with Flan, kissed her, and said, 'Happy is the bride the sun shines on,' wanting to show her my affection and give her that traditional blessing as she started her new life.
I remember saying we were almost murdered during the wedding, and Flan mentioning our throats were slashed—I could see the people in front of us gasp, shocked by what we’d revealed.
I heard Flan tell the groom that we always get this way at weddings, and I let him say it because it was easier than explaining the truth.

I became lost in a memory during the ceremony, frowning and not even noticing at first that it had ended, and when I finally realized, I felt such deep pain that I could only say, 'Oh, it was awful awful awful awful.'

I put on my best smile alongside Flan as we walked through the receiving line, congratulating the bride and groom because we had to show we were still present, even after everything we'd been through.

I remember walking into St. Peter's with Flan, the music swelling around us as we found our pew, feeling the weight of the ceremony unfolding—the quartet playing, everyone standing, the bride and her father coming down the aisle, and later joining the procession ourselves, all of it so formal and orchestrated.
I felt touched when Sandy and Connie said they were worried for me and Flan, because it showed how much they cared about us.
I remember when Sandy and Connie introduced their friend Julia, and then she said she had seen Graham Miller at Susie Baxter's, which surprised me because we hadn't expected anyone to recognize him.
I revealed that we were short by two million dollars for a deal, and I felt the weight of how much we needed Graham Miller’s help even though we hadn’t seen him in a long time.

I hosted an intimate dinner for Graham Miller, an old acquaintance from South Africa whom we hadn't seen in years, and I remember thinking how strange it was that we needed two million dollars just as he reappeared.
I told myself that having a rich friend is like being in the water while they make lifeboats, but I also knew I could never ask for one—because the moment I say the word, everything changes.

I remember how Graham Miller, a wealthy friend from our children's past, unexpectedly called and came over for dinner last night—we hadn't seen him in years, and even though Flan and I needed money, we truly enjoyed his company and weren't just sucking up.
I was at the Millbrook Club with Flan, waiting for the bride and groom to appear before the ballroom celebration, and I remember everyone clapping when they passed by our table.
I heard Flan plead with Graham Miller to leave South Africa because he was afraid Graham Miller would be killed.
I remember Graham Miller saying he had to stay in South Africa to educate Black workers, and that they’d know they succeeded when they got killed.
I joked that we’d visit Graham Miller in his gorgeous house and demand to see the poorest of the poor, wanting to be shocked, and that it felt wrong sitting on the East Side talking about revolution.
I saw Graham Miller join Flan and me in our living room, and I remember us exchanging glances, wondering how to keep the conversation going.
I heard Flan start to say he wanted to show something with the projector, but he never got to finish before we shifted gears.
I was hosting an evening with Flan for Graham Miller, and I remember rolling out the drink trolley and later getting our coats from the closet, ready to go out for dinner.
After that intense moment, I found myself pulling coats from the closet, and I remember how quickly we all turned back to figuring out where to go for dinner.
I helped pull our coats out of the crowded closet while the others sorted theirs, and I remember the clatter of tennis rackets falling as Flan handed them out.

I told Graham Miller about the man who walked into a high-end food store, bought cigarettes and an ice cream bar, and just left two twenties on the counter without waiting to pay—I thought it was a funny New York story worth sharing.
I handed the gauze to Graham Miller by mistake and took the Cezanne book from him, which caused a brief, awkward mix-up I had to correct.
I helped Flan clean and bandage Noah Kittredge's knife wound in the bathroom, following the Red Cross manual as best we could.
I went into my son's room and took a pink shirt from his bureau for Noah Kittredge to wear after we removed his bloodied one.

I saw a young Black man—Noah Kittredge—come in with a bloodied shirt, supported by the elevator man, and I remember how he said he’d been mugged in Central Park and that he knew my children, Talbot and Woody, which is why he came to me.

I remember Noah Kittredge telling me that our children spoke so highly of us, saying they were silent while other kids mocked their parents, but proudly declared that Flan and I were kind. He even said he loved Talbot and Woody, as if they meant the world to him, which made me feel seen in the way I hope parents do.
I was hosting Graham Miller with Flan that evening, and we were discussing art—Flan had just put on a Cézanne slide—when the doorbell rang, pulling us into something far more urgent.

I showed Noah Kittredge my double-sided Kandinsky, flipping it back and forth with pride as he admired both sides—he recognized it instantly and asked to see it, and I could tell he truly appreciated it, which made the moment feel special.
I refused to stay silent and named Samuel Wright as Noah Kittredge's father, even though Flan worried about libel—I didn't care, we needed the truth.
I asked Noah Kittredge if his father's wife was white, sensing it was a delicate subject but needing to know.
I remember Noah Kittredge telling me that his father left his mother for an actress named Joanna while filming 'The Lost Man,' and how he still can't bear to watch that movie.

I listened as Noah Kittredge told us about his father Samuel Wright—his childhood on Cat Island, struggling in New York, teaching himself to read, and rising to stardom—and I was captivated by how vividly he spoke, how proud and admiring he was, making me see the man behind the legend.
I heard Graham Miller ask Noah Kittredge about what it's like being Black in America, and I remember how the question hung in the air before he answered.
I listened to Noah Kittredge speak about not feeling American or even Black, and I could hear the distance in his voice, like he was describing a life he observed but didn't live.

I suggested we move into the dining room, and when I opened the double doors, I saw how the space had been cleaned and set for a formal meal, which made me feel like we were stepping into something more serious and ceremonial than before.

I listened to Noah Kittredge deliver this passionate monologue about how imagination has decayed in our culture, using 'Catcher in the Rye' as his central example—he tied it to real-world violence and the way people lose themselves, and I could feel it affecting everyone in the room, including me.
I told Noah Kittredge he would stay here tonight, in our daughter's room, and I mentioned we'd get him up early because we have a wedding in Millbrook at six fifteen.

I heard Noah Kittredge promise Flan and Graham Miller roles as humans in the Broadway show 'Cats,' and in that moment, I could see them start to see him not just as a guest, but as someone who might actually help us.
I remember Noah Kittredge asking if he had intruded, and I immediately said no—he didn't intrude at all, and I meant it, he belongs here with us.
I saw Graham Miller ask Flan to walk him to the elevator, signaling that the evening was finally coming to an end.

I remember how Noah Kittredge offered to cook for us, and I was skeptical at first, but then he transformed our kitchen into this lively, joyful space—moving with such confidence, using whatever we had, even that old jar of sun-dried tomatoes. I watched him light the Haitian candelabra and bring everything together, and I realized I was no longer just hosting a stranger; we were all part of something warm and unexpected. It wasn't just a meal—it felt like a celebration we hadn't planned but deeply needed.

I heard Flan say that Noah Kittredge's presence secured a two-million-dollar investment for the Cézanne, and that the deal with the Tokyo buyers could make us a fortune—I realized then that what seemed like a social evening had actually turned into a transaction.

I remember how our simple dinner plans with Flan and Graham Miller turned into something much more, with Noah Kittredge joining us and the whole evening shifting from casual to deeply meaningful as we moved into the dining room and shared this surprising, delicious meal together.

I told Flan to give Noah Kittredge fifty dollars, and I meant it as a gesture of care and inclusion; later, I extended the invitation for him to bring his father to dinner, because I wanted him to know he was welcome in our world.

I confronted Flan, asking why he never told me how bad things were with the money—we almost lost everything, and he waited until the last moment to say anything. I told him I'm his partner and he shouldn't shield me from that.

After we got back into bed, I held Flan and felt how lucky we were to have made it through—our life was still here, the Cezanne was safe, and I whispered that we were safe, knowing how close we came to losing it all.
I was lying in bed that quiet night, the room still, and I could feel Flan beside me, both of us lost in our own dreams, each carrying our private reckonings through the dark.

I remember dreaming of Samuel Wright sitting at the edge of my bed, and I asked him what troubled him—was it right to make a movie of Cats? He told me the world focuses too much on the beginning and end of life, and I realized he was speaking through Noah Kittredge, urging me to care about the years in between, the life we actually live.
I tapped on my daughter's door and called out, 'Noah Kittredge? Are you all right?' because I was worried about him after everything that had happened.
I remember the Hustler raising his hand and saying he might have a gun or a knife, and I shouted that he had a weapon because I was terrified.
I turned on the light and saw a naked man standing on the bed, and I screamed—I couldn't believe what I was seeing, and then he started yelling at me, and I just felt pure shock and fear.
I heard Noah Kittredge beg us not to tell his father, his voice breaking as he confessed how lonely and afraid he felt—that’s why he brought the Hustler home.
I saw Flan tip the sofa to throw the Hustler off and then force him and Noah Kittredge to leave, throwing their clothes into the corridor and making sure they took the elevator out through the back.

I looked at the clock and saw it was nearly seven, and I started wondering if Noah Kittredge was healthy after his stabbing and didn't want him to be late meeting his father, so I put down my crossword puzzle and went down the hall to check on him.

I remember shaking with fear after the break-in, clinging to Flan as we sat on the sofa, both of us drained and unable to process what had just happened—I kept thinking I couldn't be alone, I was so afraid, and when the phone rang, I begged him not to pick it up.

I overheard Graham Miller on the phone, passionately pitching his idea for a black American film festival in South Africa, naming Spike Lee, Samuel Wright, Cosby, Eddie Murphy, and Diana Ross as people he could bring in, while Flan listened from afar and I tried to catch the other end of the conversation.
I looked at Flan in amazement after we hung up, and I asked him, 'We're safe?' needing to hear him confirm it.
I got into the car with Flan and we drove away right after the call ended.
I noticed the wedding group waved goodbye to me and Flan instead of the bride and groom.
I attended the wedding with Flan, and we were there along with the bride, the groom, and the rest of the group.
I left the wedding venue with Flan after the group waved to us, and we drove away together.
I waved from the car window while Flan honked the horn, and I saw Kara and Marcus recognize us as they crossed the street.
I remember shouting to Kara and Marcus, 'Do we have a story to tell you!' at the same moment they started saying the same thing to us.
I told the detective that our two children and Noah Kittredge's son are at Harvard together.
I was sitting with the other couple at that restaurant on the East Side, the afternoon light giving everything a quiet intensity as we settled in to talk.
I remember when Flan said, 'Let me tell you our story,' his voice carrying the weight of something that had shaken him—it happened just the night before, and I could tell it still lingered.
I remember Marcus declaring that they were going to be in the movie of Cats, saying it with such certainty that it felt real in the moment.
I resolved the dispute by inviting Marcus and Kara to go first, telling them, 'You tell your story first,' and I meant it—I wanted them to have the floor after Kara's assertion.
I remember Kara interrupting Flan to insist that her story happened earlier, on Friday night, and that it should be told first.
I remember Kara telling us how Noah Kittredge was mugged and ended up staying with them, and how charming he was.
I heard Marcus describe how Noah Kittredge chased a naked blonde thief down the corridor in the middle of the night and saved their lives, and how guilty they felt because he could have been killed.
I recall Flan asking if anything was missing after the burglary, cutting in after Marcus’s story.
I met with Flan, Kara, and Marcus at Mortimer's Restaurant to talk about what happened with Noah Kittredge.
I asked Kara if she had been able to talk to her kids.
After learning they couldn't get through to their children, Flan and I decided to go back to our place.

I called Celebrity Service to find out how to contact a celebrity, trying to verify Noah Kittredge's story by checking if Samuel Wright was registered—maybe under a different name—because I wasn't sure how the service worked and needed to believe there was a way to confirm the truth.

We all came together—me, Flan, the others, and even Marcus—to try to confirm whether Noah Kittredge was really Samuel Wright's son, and I remember feeling that collective urgency as we turned to outside services for answers.
I saw Flan receive a flower arrangement from someone calling himself 'Noah Kittredge,' and when he pulled a pot of jam out of the bouquet, we all stepped back like it might be dangerous.
I said we should go to the police after that unsettling delivery because it felt like something was very wrong.
I heard the detective demand specific charges before he would take any action.
I heard my husband say that we checked the house top to bottom and nothing was gone, so I knew we hadn't been robbed.

I was there with Flan at the police precinct, and I told the detective, 'He came into our house,' because I needed them to understand what happened. I remembered how he cooked us dinner, and I could still hear Flan saying it too. I also told them about how he spoke about Catcher in the Rye and claimed he was the son of Samuel Wright—those details stuck with me because they were so strange. We gave him money, and then he left, but I kept thinking about how calmly he had been in our home, like he belonged there.
I was there when the detective told us he wouldn't do anything unless we came up with formal charges, and I felt dismissed.
I remember the string quartet playing Schubert Trio in B flat at the charity event, the music filling the room while we were there with friends.
I stood with Flan at the back of the room, telling our children and the Larkins about Noah Kittredge, and I could see the disbelief and dismay on their faces as we spoke.
I heard Tessa say I should have divorced my children just to let Noah Kittredge stay, and that he sent me flowers—her tone was so sharp, so full of sarcasm.
I wish I knew how to get hold of Noah Kittredge's father, just to see if there's any truth in what he told us.

I was overwhelmed when Marcus kept pressing me about my friend in theatrical law and whether he knew Samuel Wright—I shouted that nobody did, over and over, and we all just started screaming at each other in anguish.
I saw her storm out of the apartment in a fury, refusing to be part of what she called a 'conspiracy,' and I felt the door slam like it was closing on us.
I remember Flan pulling Tessa aside and telling her not to tell her younger sister that Noah Kittredge and the hustler used her bed.
I heard Flan tell Tessa that their family is not a conspiracy, trying to make secrecy sound like family unity.
I saw Flan take the Kandinsky off the wall and study its back, leaning it against a chair while saying he thought it was a very fine piece.
I rehung the Kandinsky painting, putting it back the way it was to restore some sense of order.

I heard Noah Kittredge deliver this intense speech about the imagination being both a warning and a guide, how it speaks to us in the dark and at noon, telling us our fears and our desires, and I remember thinking he was trying to show me something vital about how we survive our lives.
I woke up startled from a dream where Noah Kittredge hurt himself and fell, and I was relieved to find everything around me normal and safe.
I arrived at Beth Israel Doctors Hospital across from Gracie Mansion with Flan, Kara, and Marcus.
I was sitting in Dr. Lane's office with Flan, Kara, and Marcus, waiting for him to arrive.
I remember Dr. Lane coming in and explaining that he was delayed because he had been seeing a patient, and he told us he's an obstetrician at New York Hospital.
I saw Noah Kittredge after he was treated for a knife wound and some bruises, and I remember the doctor saying he was more scared than hurt.
I was there when Noah Kittredge got medical care, and I listened as the adults gathered, shared updates, and reflected on how we’re always paying off debts from our past.
I remember Dr. Lane telling me he gave Noah Kittredge the keys to his brownstone, allowing him access to the home.

I remember Dr. Lane telling me how Noah Kittredge's father, through his films, had given him direction and confidence during a time when he felt fear and self-hatred as a young Jewish man before medical school.
I heard that Noah Kittredge said something about Dr. Lane's courage in buying a brownstone with a murder history, which seemed to mean a lot to him.
I remember how we all affirmed Dr. Lane's courage after Noah Kittredge's story—it felt important to recognize that in him.
I heard that Dr. Lane was called away suddenly to help with a patient in her tenth month whose labor had just started when her water broke, and he ended up delivering twins.
I was told that after delivering the twins, Dr. Lane called his son at Dartmouth, and in that moment, he felt a deep emotional connection to fatherhood.
I found Samuel Wright's autobiography, 'This Life,' at The Strand Bookstore, and I remember showing it to the group and starting to read it right there.
I read aloud from Samuel Wright's autobiography about how his marriage was falling apart, and I could feel the room grow quiet as we all started thinking about our own relationships.
I saw Kara press Marcus, asking if Ben was hiding things, and she insisted she was going to get to the bottom of it.
I heard Dr. Lane blurt out something about crack, then quickly take it back, saying he had no proof.
I remember Flan proposing a vote on whether we should continue investigating Noah Kittredge's story, and then I voted yes when we took it, knowing we might uncover things about our children.
I remember sitting at the Gotham Restaurant with the others, trying to figure out what connected us all, and finally realizing that our children had gone to the same boarding school.

I remember how Kara read the final passage from Samuel Wright’s book, about protecting children from the truth, and then closed it in dismay—her words left me deep in thought, caught in a quiet, somber reflection with the others.
When I suggested the impostor might be a drug dealer, Doug reacted angrily and accused me of targeting him, which took me aback because I didn’t mean to imply anything about him personally.

I remember feeling frustrated when the children rejected our premise, especially when Tessa called out her father—and all of us—for assuming the impostor had to be someone from their high school involved with drugs or homosexuality, and she specifically challenged the idea that it had to be a guy.
I was at a post-lunch meeting with the other parents in Eliot House at Harvard, and it turned into a heated confrontation when the children pushed back against our questions about the impostor.
I told the children to use their yearbook to call everyone in their high school class, male or female, to find out if anyone knew a Black kid pretending to be a movie star's son.

I heard Woody scream at his parents when he found out they’d given his cherished pink shirt to the impostor—he was furious, saying it was a Christmas gift they’d bought for his new body and that he loved that shirt, and I could feel how deeply betrayed he felt.
My daughter Tessa came down to New York to bring me some important news.
I listened to the tape recording Tessa played for me, where Marcus Vale admitted he knew Noah Kittredge, and I heard it clearly when she turned it on and shared the evidence with me.

I heard that under pressure from Noah Kittredge, Marcus Vale revealed private details about my family, including where we live, our social standing, and our art collection, like the double-sided Kandinsky we own.

I heard Marcus Vale try to teach Noah Kittredge how to sound like he belonged—correcting him on words like 'bottle' and 'sofa'—and I remember Noah Kittredge repeating 'bodd-ill a bee-ya' over and over until he finally got it right, and Marcus Vale clapped like it was some kind of performance.

I remember how Noah Kittredge turned Marcus Vale's address book into a game, making him reveal secrets about people in exchange for pieces of clothing—I saw him kick over a shoe after each answer, and Marcus Vale actually seemed happy to play along.
I was told that Noah Kittredge left Marcus Vale's apartment with the address book and several of his valuables, and that it marked the end of their relationship.

I found myself thinking about how everyone on this planet is connected by just six degrees of separation, and how Noah Kittredge’s arrival in our lives made that idea feel both comforting and overwhelming.
I was with Flan and our friends at the opera, laughing and settling into our box at Lincoln Center before the performance began.
I announced to the group that we are going to Rome, feeling the excitement of changing our immediate plans.
I remember us all attending the first act of Tosca at the Met, and then moving to the champagne bar together.
I remember when Connie handed me a card with a name on it, and I passed it to Flan, feeling curious about this new connection she was introducing.
I saw Flan smile when he looked at the card, and he told me he’d call the people named on it once we got to Rome, saying he’d always wanted to meet them.
I told the art dealer that we had met someone at the opera who gave us his address.
I heard Flan gasp and say how staggering it was, and I saw how amazed he was by the scale and success of the restoration.
I stood beneath the Sistine Chapel ceiling, so close to the hand of God touching the hand of Man, and I felt awe at how vivid and clean it had become after all those years of grime.

I arrived on the scaffolding of the Sistine Chapel with Flan, stepping out of the rickety elevator in great excitement, and I remember looking up in awe at the hand of God touching the hand of Man—being this close to it was overwhelming. Our private visit, arranged by an Italian art dealer, gave us access while workers were still restoring the ceiling, with computers running the cleanup right above us.
I was at a dinner gathering in a Soho loft hosted by a man in a wheelchair and his Japanese companion, where Flan and I found ourselves at the center of attention among ten guests.
I was trying to explain what happened when the man in the wheelchair interrupted me mid-sentence, demanding to know what had happened.
I saw Flan try to dismiss the story, but the Japanese woman insisted he speak, urging him with a firm 'You must!'.
I remember when Flan and I stepped out of the taxi from the airport after returning from Rome, just before we went into the loft.
I arrived home with Flan, stepping out of the cab and back into our building, ready to return to our normal life after everything with Noah Kittredge.
I saw Frank, our doorman whom we've always treated well and tipped generously, spit directly at my husband Flan—something I can barely believe even now.
I told the audience how our doorman, Frank, whom we treat so well, actually spat at my husband Flan—it shocked me how he could do that to J. Felix Kittredge Kittredge.
I could see Flan frowning at me, and he said, 'Darling, they don't have to know every detail,' making me feel like I’d embarrassed him by sharing what happened.
I heard the Japanese Hostess ask Flan if he had a black son, bringing up that earlier accusation.
I saw Flan deny having a black son and insist that the police had brought a young girl to us instead.

I sat there with Flan, watching Elise behind the detective's desk, and I could feel the tension rise when she erupted in rage, shouting that she wanted someone dead—I’d never seen such raw fury directed so plainly.
I heard Noah Kittredge announce that his father wrote back to him, promising a thousand dollars and a meeting in Maine, and I felt a surge of hope for him.
I witnessed the emotional moment in the tenement when Noah Kittredge shared his news, talked about leaving, and bonded with Riley and Elise before his departure.
I remember Andrew teasing Flan about loving moral outrage, pointing out how his cheeks go rosy when he gets worked up, and all of us bursting into laughter.
I was with Flan at Orso's Restaurant, dining with Andrew and Jeannie after the theater performance, and I remember the warmth of the lights and the clink of glasses around us.
I heard Flan admit that he once marched in Central Park for Freedom Now, and though he meant it as an embarrassing memory, I could see the glimmer of pride beneath it.
I stopped laughing while the others kept toasting, and I could feel the mood shift around me.
I saw Elise recoil from Riley, her voice sharp as she told him not to touch her, and I noticed she wouldn't even look at him no matter how much he pleaded.
I remember Elise saying flatly that no one was to blame for Riley's state but himself, her words cutting through the room like they sealed everything.

I saw Riley pacing back and forth, pulling at his tux, clearly agitated, and he kept asking Elise if their pursuit of experience was wrong, but she wouldn't comfort him—she just pulled away and said it was all his own doing.
I remember being at that public roller skating event with Flan, and I thought we were there for heart disease or cancer, but Flan corrected me—it was actually for illiteracy.

I remember saying 'talk about six degrees' when Flan mentioned we were at the roller disco that night — yes, there we were roller skating for heart disease or cancer, though he corrected me that it was actually for illiteracy.

I remember laughing and skating faster and faster with Flan at the roller disco benefit, surrounded by middle-aged people grooving to 1940s swing music under flashy lights—it felt giddy, like we’d rediscovered something we hadn’t done in years.
I hadn't skated in I hate to tell you how many years — I said that out loud, laughing at how absurd it felt, caught in this sudden rush of joy with Flan.
I heard Flan say we came outside giddy and reeling, and I knew exactly what he meant — that dizzy, breathless feeling still spinning through me.
I met with a detective and Elise at the precinct to talk about what happened with Noah Kittredge and Riley, trying to decide whether to take legal action or speak to the media.
I arrived with Flan, Sandy, and Connie to find Riley's body lying in the street, blood slowly oozing toward the curb, and I knew he had just jumped from above—we missed it by minutes.
I heard Elise say she would press charges against Noah Kittredge because he stole their money, ruined her life, and caused Riley's death—I could feel how much she wanted him punished.
I was there when Flan proposed releasing Noah Kittredge's story to the press, directing it at me and the others, saying someone would recognize Noah Kittredge and turn him in so we could find him.

I remember Flan reading the New York Times article aloud to me, his voice full of something like pride, revealing that we’d been deceived by a confidence man and that the paper called us victims of a scam.
I was out on the terrace at the State Theatre with Flan, talking to a couple named Alex and Lily and their young ballerina during intermission.
I heard the chime that signaled the end of intermission, so I knew we had to go back inside the theatre.
I heard Flan offer to send a clipping to Alex and Lily because they mentioned missing a performance.
I made a joke about how Flan made so many copies of something that you could wallpaper the Empire State Building with them.
I remember Alex suggesting we all meet again at the same spot for the next intermission.
I heard Flan say he hadn't heard from Samuel Wright, which closed off that thread of hope for me.
I remember Flan confirming he hadn't heard from the boy either, leaving me with no sense of where he might be.
I arrived at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine with Flan in a taxi, and I saw Kara and Noah Kittredge running toward the same place.
I walked down the aisle of the Cathedral of St. John the Divine with Flan, Kara, and Marcus before the auction event.
I told Kara and Marcus we'd love to have dinner with them, but Flan and I couldn't make it because we had to work on our auction bid.
I mentioned to Kara and Marcus that we were going to a black-tie auction at Sotheby's, and Flan later said we were bidding on a second-level Henri Matisse.
I heard Flan say the bid would go well over 25 million dollars.
I stopped Flan from revealing more financial details because I knew we shouldn't say too much.

I stood with Flan in the baptistery of the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, watching our friends' infant be baptized as the priest sprinkled water on the baby's head, and I felt the warmth of the moment when everyone applauded.
I was getting dressed for the auction and talking to Tessa on the phone, going over my plans for the event I’m preparing for.
I shared with Tessa over speakerphone how I saw a sign for a store selling cruelty-free cosmetics while I was getting dressed.
I told Tessa she was not allowed to get married, that I know everyone she knows and she isn't marrying any of them—I had to make it clear I was in control.
I remember Tessa confronting me, saying it was arrogant of me to assume I know everyone she knows — the way she repeated 'I know everyone you know' like it was some kind of offense.
I put Tessa on hold because another call came in, and I needed to answer it — I said 'Wait, I'm putting you on hold' and then 'Wait. Hold on.'
I remember Tessa calling me and saying, 'Mother, I'm getting married,' out of the blue during our phone conversation.
I heard Noah Kittredge deny stealing the money, saying the boy gave it to him, and he looked afraid of being disconnected.
I heard Noah Kittredge say, 'If you put me on hold, I'll be gone and you'll never hear from me again,' and I knew he meant it—he was desperate for me not to disconnect.
I told Noah Kittredge he had to turn himself in because of the suicide, the charges, and the chance for a plea deal—I wanted him to get help before it got worse.
I remember Noah Kittredge looking at me and saying, 'Stay with you,' his voice trembling with need, as if I were the only anchor he had left.
I asked him, 'Are you suicidal? Do you have AIDS? Are you infected?'—my words sharp with fear, because I couldn't ignore how unstable and vulnerable he seemed.
I remember Noah Kittredge asking me if I felt betrayed, and he said he would hang up and never bother me again if I did — it made me realize how much he was testing whether I truly accepted him.

I heard Noah Kittredge say he had visited other hosts before us, but he didn't like them as much because they left him alone, and he specifically said he preferred me and my husband because we stayed together with him.
I recall Noah Kittredge whispering 'everlasting friendship' — it wasn't just a hope, it felt like his deepest wish, that we would remain connected forever.
I remember how tense and emotional the phone call with Noah Kittredge felt, especially with my child trying to get my attention while I was on the line with him.
I heard Noah Kittredge tell me about going to a museum, reading Warhol's diaries, and studying Michelangelo, which surprised me because it showed how much he's starting to grow.
I remember sharing with Noah Kittredge that I'd been to the top of the Sistine Chapel, and seeing his awe as he leaned into the phone, completely captivated by the idea.
I shared how they clean the Sistine Chapel frescoes—despite all the advanced technology, it's just Q-tips and water, wiping away centuries of grime to reveal vivid colors underneath.
I remember Noah Kittredge asking me so earnestly to take him to see the Sistine Chapel, his eyes lit up like it meant something sacred after I told my story.
I refused his request because I couldn't ignore that he might have murdered someone and stole money—how could I take him anywhere, let alone there?
I silently mouthed 'It's Noah Kittredge' to Flan so he would know who was on the phone.
I saw Flan decide to call the detective after he learned Noah Kittredge was on the phone.
I heard Tessa say she's getting married and going to Afghanistan, and she meant to ruin her life just to hurt her father—it struck me how desperate she sounded.
I told Noah Kittredge he was smart and stupid, and he snapped at me, shouting 'Never say I'm stupid,' making me realize how deeply he felt insulted.
I heard Noah Kittredge say his name was Noah Kittredge, with a hyphen, as if he were claiming a part of my family as his own.
I remember Noah Kittredge asking me to send him books, photos, cassettes, and letters if he goes to prison, and I said yes—I will make sure he gets them.
I remember Noah Kittredge looking directly at me and saying, 'Mrs. Lydia Kittredge Kittredge, I am black,' and in that moment, I understood the danger he was in.
Noah Kittredge said to me, 'You're just like my father,' and in that moment, I felt accused—like I was failing him the way someone else had.
I heard Flan yell at me to get off the phone with Noah Kittredge, threatening to rip it out of the wall, and I felt the weight of his fear and anger pushing me to let Noah Kittredge go.
I remember confirming our plans to go to drinks at the Pierre before the auction at Sotheby's, knowing it was one of those important evenings in our social calendar.
I told Noah Kittredge I would help him surrender to the police and find housing, and I promised to visit him and support him with kindness, though I made it clear he couldn't live with us.
I told Noah Kittredge I made a mistake and that I would come get him right away, even though I had planned to delay, because I knew I couldn't leave him alone anymore.
I remember Noah Kittredge calling me from a phone booth outside the Waverly Theater to set up a meeting with me and Flan.
I told Noah Kittredge we would be there and said, 'We love you,' because I meant it and wanted him to know we still had a future together.
He asked me to bring a pink shirt when I came to meet him, saying it with affection.
After I hung up the phone, I told Flan we could skip the social event and go straight to pick up the boy and take him to the police before heading to Sotheby's.

I attended the most luxurious dinner I've ever been to, hosted by Mrs. Bannister in honor of a United Nations dignitary, where Flan and I found ourselves recounting our strange encounter with Noah Kittredge.
I tried to stop telling the story, but Mrs. Bannister slammed her napkin down and commanded us to continue, making it clear that she was in control of the evening's flow.
I remember Flan and I calling the detective and telling them Noah Kittredge was at the Waverly Theater, even though we had promised Noah Kittredge we would bring him to the police ourselves.
I was stuck in a traffic jam on Fifth Avenue with Flan, and we were both dressed for a formal dinner we were en route to.
I saw Flan get out of the vehicle to look ahead through the noisy traffic.
I saw Noah Kittredge being dragged into a police car outside the Waverly Movie Theater, kicking and screaming while handcuffed, and I could feel the crowd watching us all.

I remember Noah Kittredge telling me that the Kandinsky is painted on both sides—a detail so specific that only someone who had truly been there could know it, and in that moment, I knew he was telling the truth about our past encounter.
I stepped forward and asked the officer if I could go with Noah Kittredge in the squad car, telling him I promised I'd take him, but he wouldn't let me near.
Flan grabbed my arm and pulled me away, insisting we leave, and I let him lead me because I didn't know what else to do.
I saw Noah Kittredge turn and look at me with an expression of betrayal as the police car drove away, and I felt the weight of that moment—he was shattered, and I couldn't stop it.
I learned from the desk clerk that the detective who handled Noah Kittredge's arrest had been transferred, which made me feel stuck and unsure how to proceed.
I asked about Noah Kittredge's arrest at the Waverly Theater, but the clerk said this precinct didn't handle anything there, so I wondered if another precinct might have been involved.
I went to the police precinct to follow up on Noah Kittredge's arrest, hoping to be there when he was arraigned because the detective had promised I could go with him.
I told the clerk that we can find anybody through six degrees of separation, trying to make him understand why I cared.
I couldn't give the clerk Noah Kittredge's full name, and when he asked if I was family, I knew he didn't believe I had any right to be asking about him.

I read today that a young man committed suicide in Riker's Island by tying a shirt around his neck and hanging himself—was it the pink shirt, that burst of color? Was it Noah Kittredge? I don't know, but I can't let go of the thought.

I remember the Guest of Honor asking me why Noah Kittredge meant so much to me, and in that moment, I realized he wanted to be us—he envied our life, our world, and he wanted to be your child, not just a visitor. I told them I wouldn’t let that go, that I wouldn’t turn him into just another anecdote we repeat at dinner parties.

I hosted a dinner with Flan, full of high-society guests including someone from the UN, and for a moment we mentioned Noah Kittredge—but then we all let social convention silence us, turning something profound into just another anecdote I’m determined not to repeat.

I stood up from the dinner table, overwhelmed by the emptiness of the conversation and how disconnected I felt from Flan and the others, and when Mrs. Bannister told me to sit down, I kept walking anyway.

I challenged Flan because I couldn't stand how he and the others were turning Noah Kittredge’s impact into just another dinner story—we were already doing it, reducing something profound to a punch line. I asked him how much of his life he could really account for, because I needed to know if he felt the weight of what happened the way I did.

I stepped into the elevator after leaving the dinner, and Flan followed me; we descended in silence until he tried to defend the importance of the guest, but I challenged him by asking what meaning his life truly had.
When I reached out to him, he just started talking about the Cezanne, the Matisse, how rich we are—I felt invisible.
I told Flan that in moments like this, I would take a knife and dig out his heart—I needed him to feel how much it hurt.
I realized then, with a strange calm, that I was smiling because it was so clear: we're a terrible match.
I gasp when I see something in a shop window, a sudden jolt running through me.

"Tell the story about the imposter who came into our lives---" "That reminds me of the time this boy--". And we become these human juke boxes spilling out these anecdotes. But it was an experience. How do we keep the experience?

I read somewhere that everybody on this planet is separated by only six other people. Six degrees of separation. Between us and everybody else on this planet. The President of the United States. A. gondolier in Venice. Fill in the names. I find that A.] tremendously comforting that we're so close and B.] like Chinese water torture that we're so close. He wanted to be us. Everything we are in the world, this paltry thing--our life--he wanted it. He stabbed himself to get into our lives. He envied us. We're not enough to be envied.

friend makes life boats. But the friend gets
very touchy if you say one word: life boat.

You see, I read today that a young man committed suicide in Riker's Island. Tied a shirt around his neck and hanged himself. Was it the pink shirt? This burst of color? The pink shirt. Was it Noah Kittredge? We never found out who he was.
I slapped God's clean hand. And you know what they clean it with? All this technology? Q-tips and water.
Absolutely. Stood right under the hand of God touching the hand of man.
our doorman whom we tip very well at Christmas and any time he does something nice for us-- our doorman spits at my husband, J. Felix Kittredge Kittredge. I mean, spit at him!

Having a heart is not the point. We were hardly taken in. We believed him -- for a few hours. He did more for us in a few hours than our children ever did. He wanted to be your child. Don't let that go. He sat out in that park and said that man is my father. He's in trouble and we don't know how to help him.
Who said when artists dream they dream of money? I must be such an artist. Bravo. Bravo.

memories.memory_text: I delivered a series of 'hello' greetings into the camera, shifting my tone each time, and when I heard clapping off-screen, I bowed in response.
I remember the rain and thunder outside, the jazz music playing, and how the white wall and the unseen presence made the moment feel both intimate and tense.
I was part of this back-and-forth with a voice I couldn't see, repeating phrases like 'bottle of beer' in a pattern that felt ritualistic, like every word had weight.
After I repeated 'bottle of beer' again, the voice told me I owed him, and I knew that moment had been building—something was demanded of me, though I wasn't sure what.
I took off my shirt and threw it at the camera—I don't know if it was surrender, rebellion, or just what he wanted me to do, but I did it.

I showed up at their door hurt and bleeding, telling them I'd been mugged in Central Park near the statue of the Alaskan husky, and that I knew their children—Talbot and Woody—because I needed them to trust me and let me in.
I saw Lydia Kittredge hand the gauze to Graham Miller by mistake and take the Cezanne book from him, which caused a brief, confusing mix-up.
I remember Flan and Lydia Kittredge cleaning and bandaging my knife wound in the bathroom while they followed instructions from a Red Cross manual.
I remember Lydia Kittredge bringing me a pink shirt from her son's room after they took off my bloodied one, and I put it on while looking at myself in the mirror.
I mentioned how your children spoke so highly of you, saying they called you kind when others were dishing out their parents, and I told you how much I came to care for Talbot and Woody too.
I remember walking into the Kittredges' apartment that evening, still dazed from the attack, and seeing them shift from hosting a refined art discussion to tending to me with real concern.
I noticed the Kandinsky on the wall and got excited, recognizing it as a double-sided piece, and I asked if I could see both sides, feeling awe as Lydia Kittredge flipped it back and forth.
I remember Lydia Kittredge asking me if my father’s wife was white, and it felt like she was prying into something painful.
I told her that Joanna isn’t my mother, that my father left my mom during the hard years after X was born, and I still can’t bring myself to watch 'The Lost Man'.

I told the group about my father Samuel Wright—how he was born in Miami during a tomato-selling trip, grew up on Cat Island feeling so poor he said they didn't even own dirt, sat by the shore dreaming of other worlds, came to New York at fifteen and a half, lived in a bus station toilet and then on the Brill Building roof, washed dishes for $4.11 a night, taught himself to read from newspapers, and eventually made films like No Way Out, Cry the Beloved Country, Blackboard Jungle, The Defiant Ones, Raisin in the Sun, Lilies of the Field, In the Heat of the Night, To Sir With Love, Shoot to Kill, and Guess Who's Coming to Dinner, winning an Oscar and becoming a top box-office star, though he once told me he still didn't fully understand how it all happened.
I remember Graham Miller asking me about being Black in America, his question hanging there, making me pause before I could even begin to answer.

I told them I never felt American—I grew up in Switzerland, at boarding school, Villa Rosey—and I didn't even know I was Black in that racist way until I came back here at sixteen; I suppose I don't feel Black either, and I know that's a kind of privilege, even if Freud would say there's no such thing as luck.

I offered to cook because I knew I could turn what little was in the kitchen into something special, and I wanted to give back—I remember opening the fridge, pulling out tuna and olives, chopping onions fast, lighting the Haitian candelabra to set the mood, and feeling the whole room shift as everyone gathered around, laughing, pouring wine, like we were all part of the same moment.
I remember we moved into the long-unused dining room, and I helped make it feel like a real event—lighting the candle, seeing everyone smile as the room came alive for a formal meal.

I joined Lydia Kittredge and Flan’s impromptu dinner gathering, which started as casual plans but turned into something more meaningful when Graham Miller came too, and we all ended up sharing food and stories in a warm, connected way.
I could see how the group was captivated by the stories I shared about my father—I felt their fascination and respect building as I spoke, and it made me glad to share those moments and memories.
I delivered a passionate analysis of 'Catcher in the Rye,' connecting it to real acts of violence and how imagination has decayed in our culture, and I could see it affected everyone in the room.
I remember Lydia Kittredge and Flan insisting I stay in their daughter's bedroom for the night, offering me care and protection after what had happened.
I told Flan and Graham Miller I could get them roles as humans in 'Cats,' and I felt them start seeing me differently—as someone who might actually help them.
I heard Lydia Kittredge tell me I didn't intrude, that I had a place in their home and in their hearts, which made me feel seen and welcomed.
I saw Graham Miller ask Flan to walk him to the elevator, and I noticed they left me alone with Lydia Kittredge.

I remember Flan announcing that I'd secured a two-million-dollar investment for the Cézanne deal, saying my presence made it happen, and suddenly the whole evening shifted from just dinner to something much more transactional.

I remember how the evening at the Kittredge home began as a relaxed exchange of ideas and food, but by the end, something deeper had unfolded—there was a financial revelation that shifted everything, though I stayed focused on making the meal and keeping the mood light.

I remember Flan and Lydia Kittredge offering me fifty dollars as a gesture of kindness before I headed off for the night—I hesitated, but I took it from Flan—and they also invited me to bring my father to dinner, making me feel like I truly belonged.
I remember handing them the money and feeling a sense of relief in the room, like we all needed that moment of connection and gratitude, even if it was brief.
I heard Lydia Kittredge call out to me, asking if I was all right, her voice full of concern as she tapped on the door.
I remember the Hustler raising his hand and saying he might have a gun or a knife, and I felt the danger in the room instantly escalate.
I was startled awake when Lydia Kittredge turned on the light and screamed—then I saw the naked man in the room and realized everything was about to unravel.
I begged my parents not to tell my father, confessing how lonely and afraid I was, because that’s why I brought the Hustler home.
The morning after, I remember dressing quickly and running into the living room with the man's clothes, knowing the fallout had already begun.
I saw Flan tip the sofa over and throw the Hustler to the floor, and then he forced both of us to leave, shoving our clothes into the hallway and making me get into the elevator.
I remember how scared I was when Lydia Kittredge and Flan confronted me, their fear and exhaustion hanging in the air as they clutched the phone, trembling after everything that had happened.
I got mugged, and Kara and Marcus let me stay with them that night because I couldn't get into the hotel until the morning.
I heard someone scream 'Burglar!' in the middle of the night, so I chased the thief down the corridor and saw the alarm go off as he ran out—I didn't know it would mean so much to them.

I stood on the ledge and spoke to Lydia Kittredge about the imagination, how it warns us and guides us, how it's the voice at 4am that tells us what we're afraid of and the voice at noon that shows us what we want, and how if we don't listen, it dies.
I remember Dr. Lane telling me how my father's career had inspired him when he was young, giving him direction and confidence during a hard time in his life.
I remember being treated for the knife wound and the bruises—they said I was more scared than hurt, and that felt true, like my body was shaking more from fear than pain.
I remember Dr. Lane handing me the keys to his brownstone, giving me access to the place.

I remember the doctor talking while he treated me, and later I heard the adults gathered, reflecting on things—something about debts and courage, though I didn’t catch all of it while I was trying to steady myself.
I remember Dr. Lane getting called away suddenly because a patient in her tenth month was in labor and her water had broken—I saw him hand me the keys before he left.
I praised Dr. Lane for being courageous to buy a brownstone with a murder history, and I could see it meant something to him.
After delivering the twins, I think Dr. Lane called his son at Dartmouth; he seemed moved, like fatherhood was echoing for him in a new way.
I calmly told the officer that Dr. Lane gave me the keys to the brownstone and that I hadn't taken anything of value—just sipped some brandy and listened to music, which I offered to make right.
I took off the silk robe and placed it on the table, then put on my jacket and walked out of the brownstone without anyone stopping me.

I was sitting in Dr. Lane's living room, listening to music and sipping brandy in my silk robe, when he walked in with a cop who had his gun drawn; I smiled at first, but then I saw the weapon and moved away, and right away Dr. Lane shouted to arrest me, accusing me of breaking and entering and calling me a fraud.
I huddled in a doorway, pulling my ragged clothes tight around me to shield myself from the freezing rain.
I noticed Marcus Vale walked past me at first, but then he came back and just stared at me, like he recognized who I am.
I found Marcus Vale's address book under him and demanded to know what it was, pulling it away when he tried to take it back.
I aggressively questioned Marcus Vale about the people in the address book, asking if they were all rich, making sure he knew I was in control.

I looked at Marcus Vale with a dare in my eyes, and I could feel the power shifting when I made him choose—names for clothes. I picked Kittredge, Talbot and Woodrow, and I made him spill their secrets: where they live, how they live, even that they own a double-sided Kandinsky.
I set up a game where I'd pick a name and he'd tell me secrets about that person, and for each answer, I'd give him back a piece of clothing.

I remember Marcus Vale telling me he didn't want me to leave him, and how he promised to introduce me to elite society as someone they'd all want to know, saying he'd make me the most eagerly sought-after young man in the East and that we'd meet again in those homes as if for the first time.
I kissed Marcus Vale, not sure if it was out of real affection or just to soften the blow before I walked out.
I left his apartment with the address book and other valuables, knowing I wouldn't be coming back.

I started picking up the way Marcus Vale speaks, practicing words like 'sofa' instead of 'couch' and saying 'bottle of beer' until I got it right—he even clapped when I finally did, and I remember feeling proud, though I know this is just the surface of who I am.
I let Marcus Vale teach me how to speak like the upper class, repeating 'bottle of beer' over and over until I got it right, even though it felt strange on my tongue.

I told Riley and Elise that I'm the son of Felix Kittredge, born from his activist past when he was down South registering Black voters, that he abandoned my mother after getting her pregnant, and that he won't see me now despite living just six windows over.
I heard Elise joke that I should say I have the Mona Lisa to get in to see my father, trying to make it seem funny.
I told them I don't want to embarrass my father—this whole thing feels so fucking tacky, and I meant it.
I asked Riley and Elise, 'You love each other?' because I needed to see how they'd react, and then I saw them touch hands.
When they asked where I live, I told them 'I'm,home' and picked up my bags—my whole life in plastic—and said, 'You're such assholes. Where would I live?'
I was with Riley and Elise in Central Park, lying on the grass near the statue of the Alaskan husky, eating and listening to Riley play his guitar while we sang along to a cheerful rock song.

I remember Riley and Elise offering me a place to stay in their small Soho loft after they found out I was homeless — they said it was over a roller disco and the space was narrow, but they insisted I could have a corner, even if the tub was in the kitchen.

I showed Riley and Elise how to speak and carry themselves so they could move through elite circles, teaching them to say 'Riding' instead of 'horse back riding,' 'sofa' instead of 'couch,' and to pronounce 'bottle' the right way.
I gave Elise some advice about not getting stuck in dead-end jobs and finding a patron, and she was really moved by it—I could feel how much it meant to her when she embraced me.
I told Riley and Elise I'm moving out of here after getting that letter, and I started packing up my things from the corner where I've been staying.
I remember Elise cutting me off as I tried to say I wanted to play Laertes—she kept listing all the roles she wanted, one after another, not even letting me finish.
I promised Riley and Elise I'd give them money to put on a play showcase with agents invited, and I told them they'll win Oscars and thank me on camera.
I burst in and told everyone that my father wrote me back—he’s going to give me a thousand dollars and we’re finally going to meet in Maine.
I saw Riley get suddenly angry at Elise when she wouldn't lend me the money, and he said she was like a stepmother holding onto the purse strings, which surprised me because he's usually so calm.

I remember how Riley and Elise listened to me, how we hugged after I promised to send money for their play, and how I started packing my bags while thinking about meeting my grandparents for the first time.
I asked Elise for $250 to get to Maine, but she refused, saying they just couldn't do it, which left me feeling stuck and disappointed.
I remember Elise kissing me goodbye, and just before she left, she looked over at Riley, who seemed upset—I could feel the weight of that moment between them.
I remember Riley and I being taken to a table by the window at the Rainbow Room, and I could tell he was impressed as we looked out over the city together.
I remember Riley looking worried, asking how he was going to explain the money to Elise.
I tasted the champagne and described its bouquet, explaining to everyone what the term means and sharing my theory that even-numbered vintage years tend to produce better wine than odd-numbered ones.
I told Riley that she'll get her money back with interest, trying to ease his mind about the cost.
I asked Riley if he wanted to dance, feeling a spark of courage as I reached out my hand.
I remember dancing with Riley, and at first no one seemed to notice, but then we drew attention and they asked us to leave—I could tell it was because we're a same-sex couple.
I led Riley in a tango on the floor, spinning him around and around, my heart lifting with joy even as I sensed people starting to notice us.

I was with Riley that night at the Rainbow Room, and I recall us dining, sipping champagne, talking about wine vintages, and then dancing—me leading, spinning him around while the orchestra played and the city spun with us.
I asked Riley if I could have sex with him—I just blurted it out—and in that moment, everything felt suddenly exposed.
I remember how I felt when he told me he didn’t do things like that—his voice was quiet, but it shut me down completely.
I kissed Riley passionately and then I jumped out of the carriage, disappearing into the night.
I remember laughing with Riley as we ran through Rockefeller Center and jumped into that hansom carriage, the city lights blurring as we started moving toward Central Park.
I heard Flan say he'd release my story to the press so someone would recognize me and turn me in — he was talking to Lydia Kittredge and the others about how they'd find me that way.

I told Lydia Kittredge I didn't steal the money—I saw the story in the paper, and I didn't even know the boy killed himself. He gave me the money, and I was scared of losing connection, of being cut off.
I told her, 'If you put me on hold, I'll be gone and you'll never hear from me again,' because I meant it—I knew that disconnecting would mean losing everything.
Lydia Kittredge told me I had to turn myself in because of the suicide, the charges, and the possibility of a plea deal, and I remember her saying I was brilliant but trapped.
I asked Lydia Kittredge if I could stay with her, needing to be close to someone who felt like family.
I heard Lydia Kittredge ask me if I was suicidal or had AIDS, her voice full of fear, and I could tell she was pulling away.
I asked Lydia Kittredge if she felt betrayed, and I told her I'd hang up and never bother her again if she did, because I needed to know she still accepted me.
I remember telling her that I only visited her and her husband because I didn't like the others—they left me alone, but with the Kittredges, we stayed together.
I said 'everlasting friendship'—that was my deepest wish, to have a bond with them that would never end.

I went to a museum and really liked Toulouse-Lautrec; I also read Andy Warhol's Diaries and Irving Stone's book about Michelangelo painting the Sistine Chapel, which made me feel more connected to art.

I remember asking Lydia Kittredge if she had seen the Sistine Chapel, and when she said she’d been to the top of it in a rickety elevator to watch the men clean it, I couldn’t believe it—I leaned into the phone, completely amazed.
I remember how tense it felt talking to Lydia Kittredge on the phone, with her child interrupting in the background, and me trying to hold onto the connection despite everything pulling us apart.
I told Lydia Kittredge how much I wanted to see the Sistine Chapel, and I asked her to take me there with her.
She refused my request, reminding me that they think I murdered someone and stole money.

I remember Lydia Kittredge telling me about how the Sistine Chapel frescoes are cleaned—she said they use simple tools, not high-tech methods, which surprised me because you'd expect such an important artwork to need advanced technology.
I saw Lydia Kittredge silently mouth 'It's Noah Kittredge' to Flan, letting him know who was on the phone.

I turned and looked at Lydia Kittredge as the police car drove away, feeling the weight of betrayal in my eyes.
