memories.memory_text: I heard Lydia Kittredge shout that the painting was gone and we needed to call the police, and I could tell she was really alarmed.
I spotted the Kandinsky leaning against the Chippendale chair and called out, 'There it is!'—relieved to find it so close by.
I saw Lydia Kittredge hang the Kandinsky with the geometric side facing out, and she seemed to admire it, like she was choosing something calmer.
I opened the office door and checked that the slide projector was still there, along with the file cabinets and other valuables, making sure everything was in place.
I remembered we had to go to the wedding later that day, so I kept my focus on resolving the situation quickly.
I remember we have to go to the wedding, and it weighs on me.
I insisted we must go, but Lydia Kittredge resisted, saying she wasn't in the mood and that they're my friends, not hers.
I called out 'Hello?' because I suddenly felt frightened, hearing something that made me think someone might still be in the apartment.
I held Lydia Kittredge tightly when she ran to me in terror after I called out, both of us scared and unsure.

I ran out of our apartment with Lydia Kittredge, my clothes barely on and my mind reeling from shock, then rushed down the side street to the garage where our Mercedes was waiting; I slipped the attendant a bill before getting into the driver's seat while Lydia Kittredge took the passenger side, and we drove off without knowing where we were going.
I remember saying out loud, 'I'm shaking,' because I couldn't hide how unsteady I felt.
Lydia Kittredge told me she would drive, and I knew she was trying to help, to take some of the weight from me.
I told her I had to hang on, that I couldn't let go, even if my hands were trembling—I needed to stay in control.
I was driving fast during the day, and Lydia Kittredge put on a tape while we were having a tense conversation.
I swerved the car abruptly to avoid a passing vehicle that veered close to us.
I remember Lydia Kittredge suddenly demanding to take over driving, saying I was driving dangerously.
I pulled myself together after losing control and moved the car over to the slow lane.
I remember Lydia Kittredge telling me she went in the room first, bringing up some earlier disagreement.
I blamed that near-accident on Maria Callas and snapped off the tape deck right then.

I saw Lydia Kittredge rush up to the bride with me, and I watched her kiss her and say, 'Happy is the bride the sun shines on,' her voice warm but somehow strained, as if the words were a duty as much as a blessing.
I remember Lydia Kittredge and I telling the guests about how we were almost murdered, and when I said 'throats slashed,' the people nearby gasped in shock.
When the groom asked if I was alright, I told him we always get this way at weddings, downplaying what I was really feeling in that moment.

I became lost in a painful memory during the ceremony, frowning and not even noticing at first that it had ended, and when I came back to myself, I felt stricken—I had to say, 'I do not always get this way at weddings,' but then the grief overwhelmed me and all I could do was whisper, 'Oh, it was awful awful awful awful.'

I remember rushing into the chapel with Lydia Kittredge, the music swelling around us as the quartet played The Wedding March and everyone stood for the bride’s entrance; I could feel the weight of the rituals unfolding, from the processions down the aisle to the moment we finally walked up ourselves and joined the receiving line, all of it so formal and bright beneath the church lights.

I composed myself with Lydia Kittredge, putting on a cheerful smile as we walked through the receiving line and congratulated the couple, making sure they knew we were present and supportive despite everything.
Sandy and Connie told us they were worried for me and Lydia Kittredge, and that’s when I realized how strange our story must have sounded as we started to share what happened.
I hosted an intimate dinner at my home last night with Lydia Kittredge for Graham Miller, an old acquaintance from South Africa whom we hadn’t seen in years.
I remember when Sandy and Connie introduced their friend Julia, and then she said she had seen Graham Miller at Susie Baxter's, which caught my attention.

I heard Lydia Kittredge say they were short by two million dollars for a deal, and I remember how she emphasized that Graham Miller might easily have that much, even if we hadn't seen him in a long time.

I remember Lydia Kittredge describing how having a rich friend is like drowning while they make lifeboats, but get touchy if you mention the lifeboat—even though we both know it's exactly what we need.

I remember how Graham Miller, a wealthy acquaintance from our children's past, unexpectedly called and asked to have dinner with Lydia Kittredge and me—it created a sudden, meaningful moment in our lives, even though the currents that night were very churny.
I was at the Millbrook Club with Lydia Kittredge and others, waiting after the ceremony as the wedding party passed by and everyone applauded before the ballroom celebration began.
I remember urging Graham Miller to leave South Africa because I was afraid he would be killed.
I heard Graham Miller say that he had to stay in South Africa to educate Black workers, even if it meant they would eventually kill him.
I recall Lydia Kittredge making a joke about how we privileged people might want to visit townships just to see the worst suffering, as if we were tourists demanding shock.
I saw Graham Miller join Lydia Kittredge and me in our living room, and I remember how we all paused, trying to keep the conversation going.
I started to tell Graham Miller I wanted to show the slides using the projector, but I didn't get to finish.
After that intense moment, I noticed everyone shifting back to talking about dinner plans and getting coats, so I helped get the coats even though I hadn't shown my slides yet.
I helped get the coats from the closet while everyone was finishing their drinks and we all agreed on going to an Italian restaurant before leaving.
I was hosting Graham Miller that evening, and I remember serving drinks, talking about old times, and making plans to go out for dinner together.
I heard Lydia Kittredge tell a story about someone stealing from Dean and DeLuca, slapping down forty bucks and walking out, probably trying to impress Graham Miller.
I saw Lydia Kittredge hand the gauze to Graham Miller by mistake and then grab it back when she realized he was holding the Cezanne book instead.
I helped Lydia Kittredge clean and bandage Noah Kittredge's knife wound in the bathroom, following the Red Cross manual to make sure we did it right.
I watched Lydia Kittredge go into her son's room and take a pink shirt from the bureau to give to Noah Kittredge after we took off his bloodied one.

I saw a young Black man named Noah Kittredge come in with a bloodied shirt, supported by the elevator man, and I turned off the projector because he said he'd been mugged in Central Park and knew our children.

I remember Noah Kittredge telling us that our children spoke highly of us, saying they praised us as kind when other kids were dishing out their parents, and how much he loved Talbot and Woody, which made me feel seen and connected to him.
I was hosting Graham Miller at our apartment, showing him a Cezanne slide and talking about the use of color, when the door opened and everything changed.

I recall Noah Kittredge recognizing our Kandinsky as a double-sided painting and showing real admiration for it, and I explained to him how Kandinsky painted in two wildly different styles on the same canvas, one geometric and somber, the other wild and vivid, while Lydia Kittredge flipped it back and forth.
I was worried about the libel risk, but Lydia Kittredge didn't care—she insisted on naming Samuel Wright as Noah Kittredge's father, saying she needed to have truth even if it meant crossing a line.
I remember how Lydia Kittredge pressed Noah Kittredge with personal questions, asking if his father’s new wife was white, and I could feel the tension in the room.

I heard Noah Kittredge say he couldn’t bring himself to watch 'The Lost Man' because that was the film where his father met his second wife and left his mother during the hard times, and it was clear how much it still hurt him.
I heard Graham Miller ask Noah Kittredge about what it's like being Black in America, and it immediately shifted the tone of the conversation.

I remember Noah Kittredge saying he didn't feel American or even Black, speaking about his privileged upbringing with white servants and life in Switzerland, and how he recognized that detachment as a kind of luck, though he questioned whether luck really exists.

I remember Noah Kittredge offering to cook instead of us going out, and then he transformed our kitchen into this lively, joyful space—chopping, boiling, lighting the old candelabra, and somehow making a meal from almost nothing. I was right there, opening the wine while he worked with such confidence, and I could see how impressed and drawn in everyone was, including me.

I remember when we moved into the long-unused dining room, which had been cleaned and set for a formal meal—I ran into the living room to bring a vase of flowers, and I could feel the shift in the atmosphere as we all smiled at the sudden elegance of the gathering.

I listened as Noah Kittredge told us about his father Samuel Wright—his birth in Miami, growing up on Cat Island, struggling in New York, and rising to stardom—and I was captivated by how vividly he spoke, how proud and thoughtful he sounded, making us all lean in, completely drawn in by his stories.

I listened to Noah Kittredge deliver this intense, passionate monologue about how imagination has decayed in our culture, using 'Catcher in the Rye' as his central example—he tied it to real-world violence, like that substitute teacher and Chapman shooting Lennon, and it really shook me, I could feel the weight of it affecting everyone in the room.
I told Noah Kittredge he would stay with us tonight, offering him our daughter's room so he'd be safe and cared for after what he'd been through.

I heard Noah Kittredge promise me and Graham Miller minor roles in 'Cats,' and I insisted that we be listed as humans in the contracts, which made me see him differently—as someone who might actually help us.
When Noah Kittredge asked if he had intruded, I said no right away—I wanted him to know he belonged in our home and in our hearts.
I walked Graham Miller to the elevator after he asked me to, signaling the end of the evening.

I remember how our simple dinner plans with Lydia Kittredge, Graham Miller, and Noah Kittredge turned into something more—how we moved into the kitchen, cooked together, and ended up sharing a meal that felt unexpectedly meaningful, though I didn’t yet know it would lead to a startling financial revelation.
I handed Noah Kittredge fifty dollars as a gesture of goodwill, and Lydia Kittredge and I invited him to bring his father for dinner—I wanted him to feel welcomed and taken care of.

I announced that Noah Kittredge's presence secured a two-million-dollar investment for the Cézanne, and I realized then that the whole evening had shifted from just socializing to something much more transactional—I even joked about giving him a commission because his connection made it all possible.
I remember Lydia Kittredge confronting me in bed, upset that I waited until the last moment to tell her how bad things were with the money—I could see she felt shut out, like I didn’t trust her.

I remember saying I wanted to get on my knees and thank God for the money, telling Lydia Kittredge I didn’t want to lose our life or the Cezanne, and then feeling her come to me—holding each other, safe, together.

I was in the master bedroom on a quiet night, lying there as Lydia Kittredge slept beside me, and though I didn’t dream of Samuel Wright like she did, I felt the weight of something shifting in the stillness—like we were both touching the edge of a truth too soft to name.
I was in an airplane hangar where a teacher was showing children's drawings under bright light, and I could feel the energy of creativity in the air around us.
I looked at the second graders' artwork and was so moved that I begged the teacher to let me study with her, even asking to join the second grade myself because I admired her work so deeply.
I asked the teacher what her secret was, and she told me she didn't have one—just that she knew when to take the children's drawings away, which made me realize how much timing matters in art.
I tapped on my daughter's door and called out, 'Noah Kittredge? Noah Kittredge?? Are you all right?'—I was worried about him, just wanted to make sure he was okay before the day really began.
I heard Noah Kittredge beg his parents not to tell his father, and he confessed how lonely and afraid he felt, which was why he brought the Hustler home.

I tipped the sofa to throw the Hustler off, and when he raised his hand and claimed he had a gun or knife, I still forced him to leave, throwing his clothes into the corridor and making sure he and Noah Kittredge exited through the back door.

I turned on the light and saw a naked man standing on the bed, and I screamed—I couldn't believe what I was seeing, and then everything spiraled with Noah Kittredge scrambling to get dressed and that man wandering around our living room like he belonged there.

I remember that morning starting like any other, with me getting up at 6 a.m., making coffee, and doing the crossword, wondering if Noah Kittredge was okay after his stabbing and not wanting him to be late to meet his father.

I remember how shaken I was after the break-in, holding onto the phone with Lydia Kittredge, both of us drained and afraid, and when it suddenly rang, we clutched each other—she begged me not to pick it up.

I was on the phone with Graham Miller when he told me he’d commit an extra two hundred and fifty thousand dollars to the bid for the Cezanne, and I remember feeling stunned—he said they’d pay, and I could depend on him for the overcall.
I was in the lounge when Graham Miller got on his phone call, pacing and talking loudly about organizing a film festival in South Africa featuring Black American artists.

I heard Graham Miller pitch the idea of a black American film festival in South Africa, mentioning Spike Lee, Samuel Wright, Cosby, Eddie Murphy, and Diana Ross to make it sound impressive, and I said it sounded like a wonderful idea.
I heard Graham Miller say he would call Samuel Wright from the Sherry, as if it were his decision alone.
I interrupted him because I needed to make it clear that we, not him, would make the call — it had to be our move, not his.
I ended the call with Graham Miller, telling him I'd see him shortly.
I mentioned my lawyer to Graham Miller, and he responded with 'The banks,' and I understood we were on the same page about something deeper.
After I hung up the phone, Lydia Kittredge and I looked at each other in amazement, and she asked me, 'We're safe?'—as if I could give her an answer that would really make it true.
I got into the car with Lydia Kittredge and we drove off, leaving the house behind after everything that had happened.
I remember Graham Miller ending our phone call and walking through the airport gate after we spoke.
I noticed the wedding group waving goodbye to me and Lydia Kittredge instead of the bride and groom.
I attended the wedding with Lydia Kittredge, surrounded by the bride, groom, and the rest of the group.
I left the wedding venue with Lydia Kittredge, driving away after the group waved us off.
I honked the horn while Lydia Kittredge waved from the car window, and I saw Kara and Marcus recognize us as they crossed the street.
I was there when Lydia Kittredge and I both announced we had a story to tell at the same moment as Kara and Marcus, right after we recognized each other.
I was told that our children and Noah Kittredge's son are at Harvard together.
I remember the four of us sitting together at that restaurant on the East Side, the afternoon light filtering through as we gathered to talk.
I started telling our story to the others, still feeling shaken from what happened the night before.
I remember Kara interrupting me, insisting that her story happened earlier—on Friday night—and that it should be told first.
I remember Marcus declaring that they were going to be in the movie of Cats, saying it with such certainty that it stuck in my mind.

I remember Lydia Kittredge stepping in after Kara spoke, resolving the tension by telling Marcus and Kara to go first—I heard her say, 'You tell your story first,' and it felt like a clear handover of the floor.
I listened to Kara tell the story of how Noah Kittredge got mugged and ended up staying with them, and I remember her saying how charming he was.
I heard Marcus describe how Noah Kittredge chased a naked blonde thief down the hall in the middle of the night and set off the alarm, and how they felt guilty because he could’ve been killed.
I asked Kara and Marcus if anything had been taken during the burglary, trying to understand exactly what went down.
I met with Lydia Kittredge, Kara, and Marcus at Mortimer's Restaurant to talk about what happened with Noah Kittredge and everything that followed.
I heard Lydia Kittredge ask Kara if she had been able to talk to her kids.
After we learned Kara couldn't reach her children and finished speaking with her and Marcus, I decided with Lydia Kittredge to go back to our place.

I remember Lydia Kittredge calling Celebrity Service, trying to find out how to contact a celebrity to verify Noah Kittredge's story, and insisting she wasn't a fan or press agent—she even mentioned my name, Felix Kittredge Kittredge, to establish our credibility.
We were all part of the effort to check if Noah Kittredge really knew Samuel Wright, and I saw how we collectively counted on that call to clear things up, even though the service refused to help.

I went to the door when the bell rang and found a flower arrangement addressed to me from 'Noah Kittredge'—and when I reached inside, I pulled out a pot of jam, which made me exclaim in confusion and made all of us recoil as if it might be dangerous.
After I showed the group the jam from Noah Kittredge's flowers, Kara said right away that I should go to the police, and I could feel the fear spreading among us.
I heard the detective demand specific charges before taking action, asking, 'What are the charges?'

I remember telling the detective how the man came into our house, cooked us dinner, told us the story of Catcher in the Rye, claimed he was the son of Samuel Wright, and then left after we gave him money.
I heard the family say they checked top to bottom and nothing was gone during my time there.
I was there at the police precinct with Lydia Kittredge when we reported the strange visitor, and I saw the detective look up from his desk as we began to speak.
I remember the detective telling us he wouldn't do anything unless formal charges were brought forward.
I was at a charity event with Lydia Kittredge where a string quartet played Schubert Trio in B flat, but I wasn't really paying attention to the music.
I took the Kandinsky off the wall and flipped it over to examine the back, leaning it against a chair as I studied it, and I remember thinking it was a very fine Kandinsky.
I heard Tessa sarcastically say that my wife and I should have divorced our children just to let Noah Kittredge stay, mocking us while bringing up the flowers he sent.
I remember Lydia Kittredge saying she wished she could get hold of Noah Kittredge's father just to see if his story was true.
I saw Tessa storm out of the apartment in a fury after the argument, and I followed her into the outside corridor, feeling helpless as she refused to be part of what she called a 'conspiracy'.
